name: Model United Nations
summary: Students represent countries in simulated United Nations committees, give short speeches, negotiate, and write resolutions together.
who: Middle school, high school and college students. Each delegate represents one country (or person or group) on one committee.
team: Individuals or pairs representing a country
length: Conferences of one to four days
resolution: Each committee has one or more topics announced before the conference.
rewards: Research into a country's real positions
Short, clear speeches in moderated caucus
start: Find a conference near you or a school club; many have beginner committees.
Read your country's statements on the topic at the UN and its government's website.
varies: No single body governs Model UN, so each conference sets its own rules of procedure, awards and speaking times.

p: Debate has two sides and a judge's decision. Model UN has many countries and the goal of a resolution a majority can pass. Delegates still need debate skills: research, short persuasive speeches, answering questions and listening for common ground.

A committee moves between **moderated caucus** (the chair calls on speakers for short turns) and **unmoderated caucus** (delegates move around the room and negotiate), then debates and votes on draft resolutions.

Model UN began as simulations of the League of Nations; the first was held at the University of Oxford in 1921. The first recorded conference called a model United Nations met at Swarthmore College in April 1947.
